challenges.name: workflow-triggers-quiz
challenges.title: Read the first CI runs
challenges.description: Three statements about what Rice Rocket saw in the Actions tab after copying a CI workflow from a blog post. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: A `pull_request` run does not test the head of the branch: look at which ref `actions/checkout` fetches for it, and at what a fork can and cannot trigger in the base repository.
Every job gets a fresh virtual machine. What does `needs:` change about when job B starts, and what does it not change about the files on job B's disk?
Read the GitHub docs on path filters and required status checks together: what state does a check stay in when its workflow never started?

questions.question:
Every commit pushed to an open pull request starts the workflow twice:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
on: [push, pull_request]
```

```text
ci  #212  feature/momo-pay  push           ✓ 3m 41s
ci  #213  feature/momo-pay  pull_request   ✓ 3m 39s
```

Statement: "Removing `pull_request` and keeping `push` is the right fix: the push run already tests the same commit."
questions.explanation: False. The `pull_request` run checks out `refs/pull/<n>/merge`, the branch merged into the current `main`: the code that will land. The push run tests only the branch head, which can pass while the merge result fails. Pull requests from forks never trigger `push` in the base repository at all. The usual fix keeps `pull_request` and limits `push` to `branches: [main]`, so a feature branch push starts nothing and a merge to main runs once.

questions.question:
The workflow installs once and tests in a second job:

```yaml
jobs:
  install:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - run: npm ci
        working-directory: api
  test:
    needs: install
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - run: npm test
        working-directory: api
```

```text
test  Run npm test
  npm error code ENOENT
  npm error path /home/runner/work/app/app/api/package.json
```

Statement: "`needs` only orders the jobs. Each job runs on a fresh runner, so `test` has to check out the code and install the dependencies itself (or download an artifact that `install` uploaded)."
questions.explanation: True. Jobs run on separate virtual machines; `needs: install` makes `test` wait for `install` to succeed and gives it access to `needs.install.outputs`, but no files. Steps share a workspace only within one job. Here `test` has not even checked out the repository, so `api/package.json` does not exist. The usual layout gives each job its own checkout + setup + `npm ci` (made fast by the cache in the next lesson).

questions.question:
The team added a path filter, and branch protection requires the `test` check. A pull request that only edits `docs/deploy.md` now shows:

```yaml
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    paths-ignore: ["docs/**"]
```

```text
Some checks haven't completed yet
  ci / test   Expected — Waiting for status to be reported
Merging is blocked
```

Statement: "The workflow was skipped by the path filter, and a required check of a workflow that never ran stays pending, so this pull request cannot be merged as it is."
questions.explanation: True. GitHub documents this: when a workflow is skipped because of path filtering (or branch filtering, or a skip instruction in the commit message), its checks stay "Pending", and a pull request that requires them is blocked. Teams handle it by not requiring that check, by running a tiny always-on job that reports the status, or by filtering inside the job instead of in `on:`. The misconception is that a skipped workflow counts as passed.

challenges.name: pull-request-workflow
challenges.title: Write the pull request workflow
challenges.description: Rice Rocket's CI file came from a blog post: it ran on every push to every branch, twice per pull request, on docs-only changes, with a write-all token and no time limit. The editor holds the corrected `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with its key blocks missing, each marked by a `# [ ]` line; some pieces are wrong on purpose. Fill every line so that: the workflow runs for pull requests into `main` and for pushes to `main`, never for docs-only changes (`docs/**`, any `*.md`), feature branch pushes or tag pushes; the token can only read the repository; `lint` checks out the code, installs Node from `api/.nvmrc` and the locked dependencies with `npm ci`, and gives up after 10 minutes; `test` starts only after `lint` passed. Run grades the file with a simulator of GitHub's trigger filters and job graph.
hints: Each test names events: a pull request into main, a push to a feature branch, a tag push, a docs-only change. For each one, which key under `on:` decides whether the workflow starts?
Look at `branches:` and `paths-ignore:` under each event, the workflow-level `permissions:` map, `timeout-minutes:` on a job, and `needs:`.

A workflow for a `web/` folder that runs on pull requests into `develop` unless only images changed: `on: { pull_request: { branches: [develop], paths-ignore: ["web/img/**"] } }`, with `permissions: { contents: read }` and a job that starts with `actions/checkout`, then `actions/setup-node` with `node-version-file`, then `npm ci`.

tests.name: Pull requests into main and pushes to main start the workflow
Docs-only changes, feature branch pushes and tag pushes start nothing
lint and test check out, install Node 24 and the locked dependencies, then run
test waits for lint, and both jobs have a time limit
The token can only read the repository
A pull request into a release branch is skipped; one touching code and docs runs
